[TABRISI:2:264/r2] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The root of turab/dust relates to soil and poverty; ذا متربة is one seated in dust from need, and ترب can also mean a peer of the same age. | mentions 90:16

[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p318#3/r2] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن قتيبة | reports | Safwan is smooth stone, wabil is heavy rain, and sald means smooth; al-Zajjaj also calls it smooth stone, while Tha'lab glosses sald as bare or clean.

[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p318#3/r4] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | The stone-and-rain image represents a show-off whose charity yields no reward on Judgment Day.
[RAZI-FULL:v7p44#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · أصحابنا | rejects | Al-Razi's school reads لا تبطلوا as a command not to perform charity in a null form: if the original motive was other than God, no valid reward ever arose to be removed later.
[RAZI-FULL:v7p44#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · أصحابنا | holds | If old and new merits do not conflict, the new event cannot erase the old; if they do conflict, the new event has no priority, and prevention is easier than reversal.
[RAZI-FULL:v7p44#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · أصحابنا | holds | A later event cannot erase what existed only in the past, what exists now without contradiction, or what has not yet come into existence.
[RAZI-FULL:v7p44#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · أصحابنا | holds | Explaining the prior merit's disappearance by the arrival of the later event is circular, since the later event requires the prior resistance already to have disappeared.
[RAZI-FULL:v7p44#2/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · أبو هاشم | reports | Abu Hashim's mutual-balancing account has each event erase some of the other; if both resulting absences occur, the causes must simultaneously exist and not exist, an impossibility.
[RAZI-FULL:v7p44#2/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · أبو علي الجبائي | rejects | Abu Ali al-Jubba'i says the later punishment alone removes prior reward; al-Razi objects that the earlier good then provides no benefit or protection, contrary to 99:7 and justice. | mentions 99:7
[RAZI-FULL:v7p44/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · القاضي | reports | Al-Qadi says the prohibition clarifies that taunting and harm cancel the reward, not the already completed act of charity; the verse compares this cancellation with a clearer case.
[RAZI-FULL:v7p44/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The first parable compares the taunting donor to a show-off who is also an unbeliever, whose reward's failure is clearer than the donor's.
[RAZI-FULL:v7p44/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The smooth stone is the unbeliever, the thin soil is the apparent donation, and the downpour is unbelief or taunting that washes away the deed's reward.
[RAZI-FULL:v7p44/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الجبائي | reports | Al-Jubba'i argues that reward and punishment cannot both be deserved because each is an eternal pure benefit or harm; otherwise the same outcome would be both just punishment and unjust denial of reward.
[RAZI-FULL:v7p45/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | If a minor sin cancels only some equal parts of reward, selecting those parts without a distinguishing cause is arbitrary; if it cancels all reward, that is rejected by agreement, so minor sins cancel none.
[RAZI-FULL:v7p45/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | If a major punishment exceeds prior reward, one part cannot be singled out to cancel it without cause; if every part independently cancels it, multiple independent causes produce the same effect, which is impossible.
[RAZI-FULL:v7p45/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Good and blameworthy consequences can coexist without erasing each other: a servant who saves his master from an enemy deserves praise but also blame for exposing the master's property to theft.
[RAZI-FULL:v7p45/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | A later act cannot alter the causal force of an earlier act in the past; absent such an effect, the earlier entitlement remains, and the past is stronger than a later event.

[RAZI-FULL:v7p47/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · أبو عبيد | reports | Abū ʿUbayd transmits al-Aṣmaʿī's view that ṣafwān, ṣafā, and ṣafwā are equivalent names for a smooth stone; al-Rāzī also defines wابل and صلد as heavy rain and barren, smooth stone.
[RAZI-FULL:v7p48#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | One reading of the pronoun says no one can recover the seed once the dust washes away, supporting al-Qaffāl's interpretation that the deed cannot benefit its giver.
[RAZI-FULL:v7p48#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | A second reading refers the pronoun to the ostentatious spender, with the generic expression functioning as a general class.

[RAZI-FULL:v7p48#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · المعتزلة | reports | On the Muʿtazilite account, God does not guide disbelievers by leading them away from reward and Paradise because of their own choices; another view glosses this as removal of faith.
[RAZI-FULL:v7p48/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The parable shows that reproachers, injurers, and hypocrites seem to have deeds, but at Resurrection their work vanishes because it was never done for God.
[RAZI-FULL:v7p48/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · المعتزلة | reports | The Muʿtazilites instead say the charity first earned reward and reproach and injury later removed it, as rain removes dust from stone.
[RAZI-FULL:v7p48/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | prefers | Al-Rāzī maps outward work to dust, the hypocrite or reproaching donor to the stone, and Judgment Day to rain; the rival reading maps reproach to rain.
[RAZI-FULL:v7p48/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · القفال | reports | Al-Qaffāl offers a seed analogy: sincere deeds grow like seed in fertile garden soil, while the reproacher's deed is seed stored on sterile stone and yields nothing when needed.

[QURTUBI-FULL:2:264#2/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | reports | One interpretation is that reminder and harm erase the gift's excellence, not its reward: a show-off earns nothing like a disbeliever, while a sincere donor originally merits reward but loses the gift's excellence.

[QURTUBI-FULL:2:264#2/r11] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | reports | The author describes ṣald as smooth, non-growing stone and gives a smooth bald forehead as an example before citing al-Asmaʿi’s verse.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:264#2/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | reports | Another view says only the reward after the donor begins reminding and harming is lost; earlier reward remains, but further multiplication stops, as charity otherwise grows like a mountain.

[QURTUBI-FULL:2:264#2/r5] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الكسائي | reports | Al-Kisa'i calls ṣafwān singular and gives ṣafwān, ṣafī, and ṣafiyy as plurals; al-Mubarrad rejects ṣafī as the plural of ṣafā, like qafā/qafī.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:264#2/r6] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · سعيد بن المسيب | reports | Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib and al-Zuhri read ṣafwān with a fatḥa on the fāʾ, a dialectal form; Qutrub also records the form.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:264#2/r7] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · النحاس | reports | Al-Nahhas allows ṣafwān to be singular or plural but judges singular more likely because the verse says dust was on it; he rejects al-Kisa'i's plural analysis as linguistically unsound.

[QURTUBI-FULL:2:264#2/r9] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Wābil means heavy rain; the same root describes a severe taking in 73:16 and severe blows or punishment. | mentions 73:16
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:264#3/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | 'They cannot do anything' refers to the show-off, disbeliever, and donor who reminds recipients: they cannot benefit from the reward of their spending when they need it, because it was for other than God.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:264#3/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Spending is called their 'earnings' because they intended to acquire a return through it.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:264#3/r3] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الماوردي | reports | Al-Mawardi says the example concerns the show-off losing reward and the donor who reminds losing the excellence of the gift.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:264#3/r4] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · النقاش | reports | Al-Naqqash says aṣlad means hairless in the Hudhayl dialect.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:264/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | 'Invalidating' means that the particular charity followed by reminders or harm is not accepted and loses reward; it does not invalidate unrelated good deeds, since sins do not annul good deeds as a general rule.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:264/r10] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The harmful donor is compared to a show-off who gives for reputation, like a disbeliever seeking praise; rain strips dust from a smooth rock and exposes its barren surface, just as these motives expose the intention and erase the gift.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:264/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | reports | Most scholars say God does not accept a donation when He knows its donor will later reproach or harm the recipient; another view says God gives the recording angel a sign not to record it.

[QURTUBI-FULL:2:264/r7] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · مالك | reports | Malik disliked paying obligatory alms to relatives for fear of seeking their praise, reminding them, or receiving repayment that compromises sincerity; he preferred strangers and having another distribute it when the ruler is unjust.

[QURTUBI-FULL:2:264/r9] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Grammatically, the comparison's kāf can be accusative as an adjective for an omitted verbal noun or can function circumstantially.

[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p650/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | The source defines صفوان as a large smooth stone and records disagreements: some use it as a collective, al-Kisāʾī gives singular/plural analyses, and al-Mubarrad rejects his proposals; Abū Ḥayyān also rejects al-Kisāʾī’s account.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p650/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | تراب also appears as توراب; ترب means becoming poor while أترب means becoming rich, the hamza removing dust/poverty.

[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p650/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | صلد is bare, smooth stone stripped of its dust; other authorities call it a bare surface, a soft stone, or anything devoid of good, and the source notes related usage for slow-boiling pots.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p661/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The prohibition repeats because the conditions already stated were not enough: reproach and injury invalidate charity, and the believers’ identity is invoked to strengthen avoidance; invalidation means no reward with God.

[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p661/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · القاضي عبد الجبار | reports | Qāḍī ʿAbd al-Jabbār argues that the charity already occurred and cannot be undone, so the verse means that later reproach cancels its future reward; Abū Ḥayyān says both readings fit, while the verse repeats warnings to stress the wrong and singles out charity because reproach is especially ugly there.

[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p662/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The pronoun in فمثله most naturally returns to the nearest antecedent, the ostentatious spender, whether hypocrite or openly boastful unbeliever; another view makes it the reproachful giver and understands two successive comparisons.
